_readme: Editorial content for the Education and young people hub (site/education/). Facts only, no advice: case studies point to verified case ids (what happened and how schools and authorities responded, from the case files); sources are measures that governments, regulators, exam bodies and international organisations have adopted or published, grouped by kind; laws are in force. Translations in config/education_i18n/<lang>.json.

laws.what_it_does: Criminalises publishing non-consensual intimate images including AI deepfakes (up to three years' prison where the victim is a minor) and requires platforms to remove reported material within 48 hours from May 2026.

laws.law: Amendment to the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes (deepfake possession and viewing)
laws.what_it_does: Makes buying, saving, possessing or watching sexually explicit deepfakes punishable by up to three years in prison and raises the maximum for creating them to seven years.

laws.law: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 138 (Sexual Offences Act 2003 ss.66E-66H)
laws.what_it_does: Creates offences of creating, or requesting the creation of, sexual deepfakes of adults without consent, in force from 6 February 2026 (images of under-18s are already covered by indecent pseudo-photograph law).

laws.law: Crime and Policing Act 2026 (child sexual abuse image-generators)
laws.what_it_does: Makes it an offence to make, adapt, possess or supply tools such as AI models built to generate child sexual abuse images, with up to five years in prison; the Northern Ireland provision checked (s.73) was not yet in force.

laws.law: Indecent images of children law as applied in UKCIS guidance (pseudo-photographs)
laws.what_it_does: Official guidance confirms that making, possessing or sharing indecent AI-generated or manipulated images of under-18s is illegal, including when the maker is a child.

laws.law: Criminal Code Amendment (Deepfake Sexual Material) Act 2024 (No. 78, 2024)
laws.what_it_does: Creates a standalone federal offence of sharing sexual material of an adult without consent, expressly including material created or altered with technology such as deepfakes.

laws.law: Code pénal article 226-8-1 (inserted by Law No. 2024-449 'SREN' of 21 May 2024)
laws.what_it_does: Punishes sharing an AI-generated or edited sexual image or voice of a person without consent by up to two years and EUR 60,000, or three years and EUR 75,000 if shared online, even if labelled as fake.

laws.law: Law No. 132/2025 on artificial intelligence (Penal Code art. 612-quater)
laws.what_it_does: Makes spreading harmful AI-generated or altered images, video or voice without consent a crime punishable by one to five years, and requires parental consent for under-14s to use AI.
Prohibits AI systems that infer emotions of people in education institutions and workplaces, except for medical or safety reasons.

From 1 January 2026 requires companion chatbot operators to disclose they are AI, run suicide and self-harm protocols, give minors break reminders, and block sexually explicit chatbot images for minors.

sources.title: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
sources.summary: UNESCO's first global guidance on generative AI in education (published September 2023, page updated January 2026) asks governments to regulate GenAI tools and build coherent policy frameworks for education and research. It proposes an age limit for independent conversations with GenAI platforms, mandatory data-privacy protection, and an ethical validation process for tools because most schools cannot yet vet them.

sources.title: AI competency framework for students
sources.summary: Sets out 12 competencies across four dimensions (human-centred mindset, ethics of AI, AI techniques and applications, AI system design) at three levels: understand, apply, create. It is meant to help curricula prepare students to engage with AI safely and to exercise critical judgement of AI solutions.

sources.title: AI competency framework for teachers
sources.summary: Defines 15 competencies across five dimensions, including ethics of AI, AI pedagogy and AI for professional learning, at three levels: acquire, deepen, create. It is built on protecting teachers' rights and enhancing human agency, and gives strategies for putting ethical principles into practice.

sources.title: Guidance on AI and children, version 3.0
sources.summary: The December 2025 update of UNICEF's policy guidance sets ten requirements for child-centred AI, including regulatory oversight, child safety, protection of children's data and privacy, non-discrimination, transparency and accountability, and building children's AI skills. It comes with a checklist for governments and companies.

sources.title: 'Deepfake abuse is abuse' (statement)
sources.summary: UNICEF's 4 February 2026 statement cites UNICEF/ECPAT/INTERPOL research finding at least 1.2 million children in 11 countries had their images turned into sexual deepfakes in the past year. It calls on governments to bring AI-generated content into child sexual abuse material laws and criminalise its creation, acquisition, possession and sharing, and on AI firms to build in safety by design and prevent circulation.

sources.title: OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026: Exploring effective uses of generative AI in education
sources.summary: Finds that general-purpose GenAI boosts task performance without real learning gains unless guided by pedagogy, and that students' advantage can disappear or reverse in exams once AI access is removed. It recommends purpose-built educational tools, equitable infrastructure and sustained professional learning.

sources.title: Committee of Ministers recommendation on AI literacy
sources.summary: Recommendation to member states to help pupils, students, teachers, parents and citizens understand AI, use it responsibly and recognise where it threatens human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It gives effect to Article 20 of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Annex III point 3 (education)
sources.summary: Classifies as high-risk AI used to decide admission or assignment to education, to evaluate learning outcomes, to assess the level of education a person will receive, and to monitor and detect prohibited behaviour by students during tests. High-risk systems carry obligations such as risk management, human oversight and documentation.

sources.title: Ethical guidelines on the use of AI and data in teaching and learning for educators (updated)
sources.summary: First issued in 2022 and updated in 2026 through the European Digital Education Hub, the guidelines explain the GDPR and AI Act context for teachers. They provide guiding questions and case examples for judging AI tools before using them in class.

sources.title: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education
sources.summary: DfE policy (updated August 2025) says safety should be the top priority, pupils should use GenAI only with safeguards such as supervision and filtering and monitoring, and personal data should not be put into GenAI tools. It warns GenAI can make cyber attacks and impersonation emails more credible and points to JCQ and Ofqual rules on AI malpractice.

sources.title: Generative AI: product safety standards
sources.summary: Standards for edtech suppliers (first issued January 2025, expanded 19 January 2026) covering filtering, monitoring and reporting to the safeguarding lead, security against jailbreaking, privacy, testing and governance. The 2026 update adds cognitive development, emotional and social development, mental health and anti-manipulation standards, including avoiding anthropomorphism and emotional dependence and detecting distress.

sources.title: Cyber security standards for schools and colleges
sources.summary: Sets standards including annual cyber risk assessment, staff and student training, MFA for staff cloud/remote and admin accounts, patching critical vulnerabilities within 14 days, and a 3-2-1 style backup plan. It also requires reporting cyber attacks internally and to bodies such as insurers and the DfE (last updated September 2026).

sources.organisation: UK Council for Internet Safety / DfE
sources.title: Sharing nudes and semi-nudes: advice for education settings working with children and young people
sources.summary: The March 2024 update explicitly covers AI-generated and digitally manipulated 'pseudo-images' of under-18s and says the law applies to children who make them. It tells staff to refer to the designated safeguarding lead, avoid viewing, copying or sharing images, refer to police or social care where needed, and use removal tools such as IWF/Childline Report Remove.

sources.title: Keeping children safe in education 2026
sources.summary: Statutory safeguarding guidance for schools and colleges, with the 2026 version in force from 1 September 2026. DfE's GenAI guidance names it as the core reference for online safety, filtering and monitoring and cyber security when schools use AI.

sources.title: AI Use in Assessments: Your role in protecting the integrity of qualifications
sources.country_or_scope: UK (GCSE, A level and other general qualifications)
sources.summary: Guidance effective 30 April 2025 treats AI misuse that leaves work not the student's own as malpractice and requires centres' malpractice policies to cover AI. It recommends supervised in-class work, checking drafts, short viva-style discussions and restricting AI on centre devices, says detectors must not be relied on alone, and says AI cannot be the sole marker.

sources.organisation: Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education (QAA)
sources.title: Maintaining quality and standards in the ChatGPT era: advice on generative AI tools
sources.summary: QAA advises universities that managed use of generative AI is preferable to outright bans, while maintaining academic standards. It offers a four-step process for identifying assessments that need adjusting and urges robust internal quality assurance.

sources.organisation: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA)
sources.title: Enacting assessment reform in a time of artificial intelligence
sources.summary: Non-prescriptive TEQSA resource (released September 2025) that helps universities manage generative AI risks to the assurance of learning while teaching ethical use. It maps the main strategic pathways institutions are taking to redesign assessment.

sources.title: Essex school reprimanded after using facial recognition technology for canteen payments
sources.summary: The ICO reprimanded Chelmer Valley High School (23 July 2024) for introducing facial recognition without a data protection impact assessment, without consulting its DPO, parents or pupils, and relying on opt-out consent. It stresses a DPIA is required before biometric systems and that explicit opt-in consent is needed.

sources.title: Determination on biometric identifying technology in schools
sources.summary: The September 2023 determination bars New York schools from buying or using facial recognition technology, after a state report found the risks outweighed benefits, including higher misidentification rates for children and other groups. Other biometric tools are left to local decisions that must weigh privacy, civil rights, effectiveness and parental input.

sources.organisation: US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
sources.title: Protecting Our Future: Partnering to Safeguard K-12 Organizations from Cybersecurity Threats
sources.summary: CISA's January 2023 report tells schools to start with the most impactful measures: MFA, patching known exploited vulnerabilities, tested backups, an exercised incident response plan and ongoing training. It also urges pressing vendors for secure-by-default products and joining information-sharing groups such as MS-ISAC and K12 SIX.

sources.title: Senior US Officials Impersonated in Malicious Messaging Campaign (PSA I-051525-PSA)
sources.summary: Warns that criminals are using AI-generated voice messages and texts to impersonate senior officials and steal account access. It advises verifying identity through a known number, not clicking links until verified, enabling two-factor authentication, using agreed code words, and confirming payment requests through a separate channel.

sources.title: FTC launches inquiry into AI chatbots acting as companions
sources.summary: On 11 September 2025 the FTC ordered seven firms, including Alphabet, Character.AI, Meta, OpenAI, Snap and xAI, to explain how they test, monitor and limit harms of companion chatbots to children. It asks about monetising engagement, age-restriction enforcement, disclosures to parents and use of conversation data.

sources.title: Toolkit for Schools: Guide to responding to image-based abuse involving AI deepfakes
sources.summary: Step-by-step guide (first released mid-2025, current PDF dated March 2026) for school leaders responding to nude or sexual deepfakes of students or staff, designed to sit alongside child-protection policies. eSafety urges schools to prioritise the wellbeing of targeted students and staff, report possible crimes to police, meet mandatory reporting duties and use eSafety for rapid removal.

sources.title: Online safety advisory: AI chatbots and companions - risks to children and young people
sources.summary: The 18 February 2025 advisory warns that AI companions simulate personal relationships, allow unregulated discussion of sex, self-harm and suicide, and often lack effective age checks. eSafety later issued legal notices (October 2025) to Character.AI, Nomi, Chai and Chub AI and reported that most companions failed to refer users to support for suicide or self-harm.

sources.organisation: Republic of Korea Ministry of Education (reported by The Korea Herald)
sources.title: Education Ministry response to school deepfake sex crimes
sources.summary: In August 2024 the ministry set up an emergency task force to track school deepfake cases weekly, handle victim reports, give psychological support and strengthen digital-ethics education. It said high-school perpetrators could face expulsion, the top sanction in the school-violence system.

sources.organisation: Republic of Korea Ministry of Education (reported by The Korea Times)
sources.title: 799 students, 31 teachers victimized by deepfake videos this year
sources.summary: Ministry survey data showed 833 school victims of deepfakes in 2024 to late October, including 799 students and 31 teachers. Schools referred 417 cases for investigation and 218 for deletion of videos.

sources.organisation: Ireland Department of Education and Youth
sources.title: Guidance on Artificial Intelligence in Schools
sources.summary: National guidance published 21 October 2025 with Oide to help schools plan safe, ethical and appropriate AI use, drawing on UNESCO and EU work. It notes the State Examinations Commission requires AI-generated material to be referenced, and a taskforce on AI in education including assessment was announced.

sources.organisation: UAE Ministry of Education (reported by Education Middle East)
sources.title: Safe and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in Classrooms (manual)
sources.summary: The 2026 manual bans generative AI for students under 13 or below Year 7, bans AI in formal exams and undisclosed AI work, and prohibits entering personal data of students, teachers or parents into AI tools. It also prohibits deepfakes and impersonation and requires direct teacher oversight of classroom AI use.

sources.organisation: Saudi Ministry of Education and SDAIA (reported by Gulf News)
sources.title: Guidelines for using generative AI in education
sources.summary: Joint guidebook for students, teachers and parents aimed at ethical and responsible use that keeps the teacher central. It says students under 13 should not use GenAI without direct supervision and under-18s need clear parental consent.

sources.organisation: Center for Educational Research and Development (CRDP), Lebanon
sources.title: Lebanon's AI Competency Framework / AI Educational Framework for students and teachers
sources.summary: CRDP, which develops Lebanon's national curriculum, published (October 2025) an AI framework whose first part is an AI policy for Lebanese schools built on UNESCO's 2024 frameworks and 2021 AI ethics recommendation. Its guiding principles include a human-centred approach, data privacy and security, inclusivity and teacher professional development.

sources.organisation: Egypt Ministry of Education and Technical Education (reported by Egyptian Streets)
sources.title: AI curricula in schools from 2025-2026
sources.summary: The minister announced AI curricula in selected primary, preparatory and secondary grades from 2025-26, including the ethics and social implications of AI. No published usage or safeguarding guideline from the ministry was found.
